title: Predicting Post-Graduation Earnings Using Tuition, Institutional Metrics, and Student Demographics
text:
Overview

Goal: Understand how tuition, financial burden, and institutional characteristics relate to post-graduation earnings.
Data: U.S. Department of Education College Scorecard (bachelor’s-degree-granting institutions).
Methods:

Exploratory data analysis
Linear & Ridge regression
Logistic regression & Random Forest
Feature selection & permutation importance

Key focus: Which institutional features most strongly predict higher earnings 10 years after enrollment?

title: Predicting Post-Graduation Earnings Using Tuition, Institutional Metrics, and Student Demographics
text:
Research Questions

RQ1. How do tuition and financial burden relate to median earnings 10 years after enrollment?
RQ2. How do institutional characteristics (region, locale, control, size) and student composition (Pell share) relate to earnings and completion?
RQ3. Can institutional features reliably classify colleges as high-earning vs. low-earning?
RQ4. Which features are most important for prediction across linear and machine-learning models?

title: Predicting Post-Graduation Earnings Using Tuition, Institutional Metrics, and Student Demographics
text:
Data & Preprocessing

Source: U.S. College Scorecard (institution-level data).
Scope:

Filtered to institutions that primarily award bachelor’s degrees.
Focused on recent cohorts with available 10-year earnings.

Key variable groups:

Cost: in-state & out-of-state tuition, median debt.
Institutional: enrollment (UGDS), control, region, locale.
Outcomes: retention, 4-year completion, 10-year median earnings.

Missing data:

Dropped columns with severe missingness (e.g., detailed demographics).
Dropped rows with missing core cost/outcome variables rather than imputing.

title: Predicting Post-Graduation Earnings Using Tuition, Institutional Metrics, and Student Demographics
text:
Sample Structure Check

Compared original vs. cleaned distributions for:

State, region, locale, and control type.

Result: Filtering and missing-data removal:

Did not wipe out any region or control group.
Preserved a broad mix of public and private institutions across the U.S.

Interpretation: The cleaned dataset still represents a diverse institutional landscape.

title: Predicting Post-Graduation Earnings Using Tuition, Institutional Metrics, and Student Demographics
text:
Exploratory Data Analysis

Cost:

In-state and out-of-state tuition are right-skewed.
Most schools between ≈ $10K–$40K; a small number of very expensive institutions.

Size (UGDS):

Strong right skew; most enroll 1K–6K students.
A few very large institutions (e.g., large online providers).

Outcomes:

Retention and completion rates are bounded [0,1] and cluster toward higher values.
Identified and removed institutions with impossible patterns (e.g., 0% completion at all time horizons, 0% retention with missing context).

Earnings:

10-year earnings percentiles are skewed; median earnings used as a stable target.

title: Predicting Post-Graduation Earnings Using Tuition, Institutional Metrics, and Student Demographics
text:
Correlation Patterns

Tuition has only weak to moderate correlation with earnings.
Retention and completion rates show moderate positive correlations with earnings.
Pell Grant share (PCTPELL) shows negative correlations with both earnings and completion:

Institutions serving more low-income students tend to have lower median earnings.

Takeaway: Institutional performance and student composition are more strongly related to outcomes than tuition alone.

title: Predicting Post-Graduation Earnings Using Tuition, Institutional Metrics, and Student Demographics
text:
Regression Setup

Target: Median earnings 10 years after enrollment (MD_EARN_WNE_P10).
Predictors:

Cost: TUITIONFEE_IN, TUITIONFEE_OUT, median debt.
Institution: UGDS, region dummies, locale dummies, control dummies.
Outcomes: retention and completion rates.

Preprocessing:

Log-transform skewed variables where appropriate.
Standardize continuous predictors.
One-hot encode categorical variables (region, locale, control).

title: Predicting Post-Graduation Earnings Using Tuition, Institutional Metrics, and Student Demographics
text:
Linear & Ridge Regression Results

Linear model (OLS):

Adjusted R² ≈ 0.57 — institutional features explain ~57% of variance in earnings.
Strong positive coefficients: in-state tuition, retention, 4-year completion.
Strong negative coefficients: median debt, Pell share, several lower-wage regions.

Multicollinearity:

High VIF for tuition variables → removed out-of-state tuition for OLS.
Ridge regression refit with both tuition variables:

Similar R² (~0.49 on test data).
More stable coefficients in the presence of collinearity.


Limitations:

Residuals show curvature, heteroscedasticity, and heavy tails → linear model is an approximation.

title: Predicting Post-Graduation Earnings Using Tuition, Institutional Metrics, and Student Demographics
text:
Feature Selection for Classification

Outcome for classification: High-earning vs. low-earning institution
(above vs. below sample median earnings).
Feature selection strategy:

SelectKBest (f_classif) to identify top 15 statistically relevant predictors.
Random Forest feature importance to capture nonlinear effects and interactions.
Final feature set = union of the top features from both methods.

Self-taught component:

Added permutation importance to quantify how much model performance drops when each feature is shuffled.

title: Predicting Post-Graduation Earnings Using Tuition, Institutional Metrics, and Student Demographics
text:
Logistic Regression Classification

Model: Logistic regression with standardized predictors.
Performance:

Accuracy ≈ 0.77
Precision ≈ 0.78
Recall ≈ 0.77
F1 ≈ 0.77
5-fold CV F1 ≈ 0.80

Interpretation:

A simple linear decision boundary separates high- and low-earning institutions reasonably well.
Coefficient patterns mirror regression results: retention, completion, tuition, and Pell share are key drivers.

title: Predicting Post-Graduation Earnings Using Tuition, Institutional Metrics, and Student Demographics
text:
Random Forest Classification

Model: Random Forest classifier using the selected feature set.
Performance:

Accuracy ≈ 0.78
Precision, Recall, F1 ≈ 0.78
5-fold CV F1 ≈ 0.82

Insights:

Slightly better predictive performance than logistic regression.
Captures nonlinear relationships and interactions among:

Enrollment size (UGDS)
Retention and completion
Tuition levels
Pell share
Certain regions

title: Predicting Post-Graduation Earnings Using Tuition, Institutional Metrics, and Student Demographics
text:
Permutation Importance (Random Forest)

Top predictors for high-earning institutions:

UGDS (student body size)
RET_FT4 (first-year retention)
TUITIONFEE_OUT and TUITIONFEE_IN
PCTPELL (share of Pell recipients)
Regional indicators (e.g., Southeast, Mid East)

Low-impact features:

Many fine-grained locale categories
Control type contributes relatively little once other factors are included.

Takeaway: Structural and academic characteristics (size, retention, completion) and student composition matter more than geographic setting.

title: Predicting Post-Graduation Earnings Using Tuition, Institutional Metrics, and Student Demographics
text:
Calibration: Probabilities vs. Accuracy

Calibration curve comparison:

Logistic regression:

Probabilities closely follow the 45° line → well-calibrated.
Predicted probabilities match observed frequencies.

Random Forest:

Produces extreme probabilities (mostly near 0 or 1).
Overconfident and poorly calibrated without post-processing.


Implication:

Random Forest is better for classification accuracy.
Logistic regression is better when probability estimates are used for decision-making or interpretation.

title: Predicting Post-Graduation Earnings Using Tuition, Institutional Metrics, and Student Demographics
text:
Key Findings

Higher tuition is associated with higher earnings, but:

Effects are modest and intertwined with other institutional features.

Retention and completion rates are strong, consistent predictors of long-term earnings.
Institutions with higher Pell Grant shares tend to have lower earnings, reflecting underlying socioeconomic differences.
Model performance:

Linear and Ridge regression explain ~50–57% of earnings variation.
Classification models distinguish high- vs low-earning institutions with F1 ≈ 0.77–0.82.

Student outcomes and composition matter at least as much as sticker price.

title: Predicting Post-Graduation Earnings Using Tuition, Institutional Metrics, and Student Demographics
text:
Limitations & Future Work

Data limitations:

Institution-level aggregates; no student-level or major-level detail.
Missing data and reporting differences across institutions.

No causal claims:

Observational, cross-sectional analysis; cannot separate institution effect from selection bias.

Future directions:

Incorporate program/major mix and selectivity.
Explore causal methods or matching designs.
Examine changes over time (longitudinal trends).

title: Predicting Post-Graduation Earnings Using Tuition, Institutional Metrics, and Student Demographics
text:
Takeaways

Tuition alone is an incomplete indicator of value.
Academic success metrics (retention & completion) and student demographics are central to explaining earnings.
Machine-learning models provide modest gains in accuracy over linear models but highlight similar core drivers.
For policy, student advising, or institutional benchmarking, interpreting both cost and outcomes together is essential.

title: Impact of Tuition and Financial Aid on Student Retention and Post-Graduation Outcomes
text: This project investigates how tuition, financial aid indicators, and institutional characteristics relate to student retention and post-graduation earnings using the U.S. College Scorecard dataset. After filtering the data to bachelor’s-degree-granting institutions and performing extensive preprocessing, exploratory analysis revealed substantial variation in cost, student composition, and outcomes across institutions. Linear and Ridge regression models were used to estimate relationships with median earnings ten years after enrollment, while logistic regression and random forest classifiers predicted whether an institution fell above the national median earnings level. Results show that retention, completion rates, tuition, institutional size, and Pell Grant share are among the strongest predictors of outcomes. These findings highlight the combined influence of cost, socioeconomic composition, and institutional performance on long-term student success.

text:
Dataset
A brief description of your dataset including its provenance, dimensions, etc. as well as the reason why you chose this dataset.
Make sure to load the data and use inline code for some of this information.
This data contains institution-level data files for 1996-97 through 2022-23 containing aggregate data for each institution. Includes information on institutional characteristics, enrollment, student aid, costs, and student outcomes. Field of study-level data files for the pooled 2014-15, 2015-16 award years through the pooled 2018-19, 2019-20 award years containing data at the credential level and 4-digit CIP code combination for each institution. Includes information on cumulative debt at graduation and earnings one year after graduation. Essentially, this dataset holds a lot of information that can be used to understand student success, university statistics, and demographic information.
Initialy, this dataset contains 3306 columns, and 6430 rows. Since this file is too large to load directly into Github, I am working on solutions. Thus, I do have have robust numbers and have yet to clean and throw columns that I am not interested in. I will be retaining a lot of columns related to the cost of attendance, demographic information, and outcome metrics which indclude salary metric, retention percentages, etc.
The main columns I will be considering are outlined below: - INSTNM: Institution name - STABBR: 2-letter state abbreviation - HIGHDEG: Highest degree awarded: 0 Non-degree-granting 1 Certificate degree 2 Associate degree 3 Bachelor’s degree 4 Graduate degree - PREDEG: Predominant undergraduate degree awarded: 0 Not classified 1 Predominantly certificate-degree granting 2 Predominantly associate’s-degree granting 3 Predominantly bachelor’s-degree granting 4 Entirely graduate-degree granting - CONTROL: Control of institution (IPEDS) (i.e. private, public) - COSTT4_A: Average cost of attendance (academic year institutions) - TUITIONFEE_IN: In-state tuition and fees - TUITIONFEE_OUT: Out-of-state tuition and fees - TUITFTE: Net tuition revenue per full-time equivalent student - C150_4: Completion rate for first-time, full-time students at four-year institutions (150% of expected time to completion) - C150_4_POOLED: Completion rate for first-time, full-time students at four-year institutions (150% of expected time to completion), pooled for two year rolling averages - RET_FT4: First-time, full-time student retention rate at four-year institutions - COMP_ORIG_YR4_RT: Percent completed within 4 years at original institution - COMP_ORIG_YR6_RT: Percent completed within 6 years at original institution - RPY_1YR_RT: Fraction of repayment cohort who are not in default, and with loan balances that have declined one year since entering repayment, excluding enrolled and military deferment from calculation. (Rolling averages) - DEP_INC_AVG: Average family income of dependent students in real 2015 dollars. - GRAD_DEBT_MDN: The median debt for students who have completed - COUNT_WNE_P10: Number of students working and not enrolled 10 years after entry - MD_EARN_WNE_P10: Median earnings of students working and not enrolled 10 years after entry - COUNT_WNE_INC1_P10: Number of students working and not enrolled 10 years after entry in the lowest income tercile $0-$30,000 - COUNT_WNE_P6: Mean earnings of students working and not enrolled 6 years after entry - MD_EARN_WNE_P6: Median earnings of students working and not enrolled 6 years after entry - COUNT_WNE_INC1_P6: Number of students working and not enrolled 6 years after entry in the lowest income tercile $0-$30,000
I chose this dataset because it allows me to directly link financial inputs (tuition and aid) with student outcomes (retention and earnings), helping to uncover whether affordability or institutional prestige has a stronger effect on student success. Additionally, this dataset holds so much interesting data, and I am interested in a lot of these columns. However, I will need to balance the number of columns I look at and the my main goals for the project.

Questions
The two questions you want to answer.

How does average cost of attendance aid affects student retention rates at institutions with different tuition levels?
Is there a relationship between institutional tuition and post-graduation earnings, and does this differ by institution type (public, private nonprofit, for-profit)?

title: Predicting Post-Graduation Earnings Using Tuition, Institutional Metrics, and Student Demographics
text:
Analysis plan

A plan for answering each of the questions including the variables involved, variables to be created (if any), external data to be merged in (if any).

To answer the first question, I will be looking at the average net prices and retention. There are multiple columns for each of these factors in the dataset. Next, there are several breakdowns concerning the percentage of student working after graduation. I will use this data and compare the type of institution and the tuition to see if there is a relationship. I plan on doing an EDA and determining which factors specifically I want to focus on, then I will perform a linear regression if that makes sense for the data, or other forms of quantitative analysis in order to determine a relationship.
